title: Die Geschichte vom wilden Jäger
titleEn: The Story of the Wild Huntsman
source: Heinrich Hoffmann, Der Struwwelpeter, Rütten & Loening, Frankfurt am Main, 564. Auflage — the canonical later text in modernized spelling (via Project Gutenberg #24571). Fresh Lectorium translation from the German.
about: The one piece in Heinrich Hoffmann’s 1845 book with no naughty child in it at all: the wild huntsman falls asleep in the sun, the hare takes his gun and his spectacles and turns hunter, and the chase runs backwards through a well, a coffee cup and a scalded young hare. The title glances at »der wilde Jäger«, the spectral huntsman of German legend, which sharpens the deflation — this one is undone by a rabbit and his own heavy gun. It is the book’s pure farce: no moral is drawn, nobody is punished, and the poem simply stops.

sentences.t:
Es zog der wilde Jägersmann
sein grasgrün neues Röcklein an;
sentences.l:
There pulled the wild huntsman
his grass-green new little-coat on;
sentences.i:
The wild huntsman pulled on
his new grass-green coat;
sentences.n: »anziehen« (‘to put on’) is separable, and the »an« has to wait out a line and a half before it lands, at the rhyme — the tailor’s »ab« all over again. The placeholder »es« fills the front slot so the subject can follow the verb. »der Jägersmann« is the folk-song form of »Jäger«. Green is the hunter’s colour, then as now; »Röcklein« is the -lein diminutive — his little coat, and the diminutive is already laughing at him.

sentences.t:
nahm Ranzen, Pulverhorn und Flint
und lief hinaus ins Feld geschwind.
sentences.l:
took satchel, powder-horn and gun
and ran out into-the field swiftly.
sentences.i:
took his knapsack, powder horn and musket,
and ran off out into the fields.
sentences.n: The subject is simply dropped and the verbs chain on to it (the dog at the well did the same). The three nouns come without articles, read off like an inventory. »die Flint« is »die Flinte«, the muzzle-loading fowling piece of the period — the powder horn is what you charge it from. »hinaus« = ‘out, away from here’; »geschwind« = ‘swiftly’, old-fashioned now.

sentences.t:
Er trug die Brille auf der Nas
und wollte schießen tot den Has.
sentences.l:
He wore the spectacles on the nose
and wanted to-shoot dead the hare.
sentences.i:
He wore his spectacles on his nose
and meant to shoot the hare dead.
sentences.n: »die Brille« is singular in German — one pair, one word. Article and no possessive for the body part again (»auf der Nas«, clipped from »Nase«). The word order of the second line is bent as far as it will go for the rhyme: plain prose would be »und wollte den Hasen totschießen«, with the separable »tot-« welded to the front of the verb and the whole thing at the end. »der Has« = »der Hase«.

sentences.t:
Das Häschen sitzt im Blätterhaus
und lacht den wilden Jäger aus.
sentences.l:
The little-hare sits in-the leaf-house
and laughs the wild huntsman out.
sentences.i:
The little hare sits in his house of leaves
and laughs at the wild huntsman.
sentences.n: »auslachen« is separable — »lacht … aus« = ‘to laugh at, to mock’, with the »aus« at the end as usual. »das Blätterhaus« is Hoffmann’s own coinage: the hare’s house of leaves. And the tense turns present for the hare, who from here on does everything in front of your eyes while the huntsman is narrated in the past.

sentences.t:
Jetzt schien die Sonne gar zu sehr,
da ward ihm sein Gewehr zu schwer.
sentences.l:
Now shone the sun far too much,
there became to-him his gun too heavy.
sentences.i:
Now the sun shone far too hot,
and his gun grew too heavy for him.
sentences.n: »ward« is the old past of »werden« (‘became’), where modern German says »wurde« — pure storybook. »gar zu sehr« = ‘far too much’, with »gar« intensifying as it does throughout this book. »ihm« is the dative of the person affected: heavy *for him*.

sentences.t:
Er legte sich ins grüne Gras;
das alles sah der kleine Has.
sentences.l:
He laid himself into the green grass;
that all saw the little hare.
sentences.i:
He lay down in the green grass;
the little hare saw all of it.
sentences.n: »sich legen« = ‘to lay oneself down.’ »ins grüne Gras« takes the accusative because it is motion into; at the end of the poem the young hare sits »im grünen Gras«, dative, because he is merely there. »Das alles« is fronted for weight: ‘all of that, the little hare saw.’

sentences.t:
Und als der Jäger schnarcht und schlief,
der Has ganz heimlich zu ihm lief
und nahm die Flint und auch die Brill
und schlich davon ganz leis und still.
sentences.l:
And when the huntsman snores and slept,
the hare quite secretly to him ran
and took the gun and also the spectacles
and crept away quite soft and still.
sentences.i:
And while the huntsman snored and slept,
the hare ran up to him in secret
and took the gun and the spectacles too,
and stole away, soft and still.
sentences.n: »schnarcht und schlief« sets a present beside a past inside one clause, which no prose would allow; the rhyme wanted »schlief«. »davonschleichen« is separable: »schlich davon« = ‘crept away.’ »die Brill« is »die Brille« clipped, like »Flint« and »Has«. And after the »als«-clause the main clause keeps its subject in front of the verb (»der Has … lief«) instead of inverting, as prose would require — verse licence.

sentences.t:
Die Brille hat das Häschen jetzt
sich selbst auf seine Nas gesetzt;
sentences.l:
The spectacles has the little-hare now
on his very own nose set;
sentences.i:
The little hare has now set the spectacles
on his own nose;
sentences.n: The object stands first and the participle »gesetzt« waits at the very end, with the whole sentence packed between the two halves of the verb — that bracket is the shape of a German perfect. »sich selbst« = ‘on his own self.’ The hare now has the gun and the eyes both.

sentences.t:
und schießen will's aus dem Gewehr.
Der Jäger aber fürcht sich sehr.
sentences.l:
and shoot wants it out of the gun.
The huntsman however is greatly afraid.
sentences.i:
and he means to fire the gun.
But the huntsman is terribly afraid.
sentences.n: »will’s« = »will es«, and the »es« is there because »das Häschen« is neuter, exactly as »das Mohrchen« was; English has to say ‘he.’ »sich fürchten« = ‘to be afraid’, with »fürcht« clipped from »fürchtet«. »sich sehr fürchten« is ordinary German for being badly frightened — this is the everyday »sehr«, not the older ‘sorely’ that »da schreit der Konrad sehr« carries.

sentences.t:
Er läuft davon und springt und schreit:
»Zu Hilf, ihr Leut, zu Hilf, ihr Leut!«
sentences.l:
He runs away and leaps and screams:
“To help, you folk, to help, you folk!”
sentences.i:
He runs off, leaping and screaming:
“Help, good people, help, good people!”
sentences.n: »davonlaufen« separable again: »läuft davon«. »zu Hilf!« is »zu Hilfe!« clipped — the same cry the cats raised over Paulinchen. »ihr Leut« = »ihr Leute«, ‘you people’: what you shouted in a village street when you wanted anyone at all to come.

sentences.t:
Da kommt der wilde Jägersmann
zuletzt beim tiefen Brünnchen an.
sentences.l:
There comes the wild huntsman
at last at-the deep little-well up.
sentences.i:
At last the wild huntsman
comes up to the deep little well.
sentences.n: »ankommen« (‘to arrive’) is separable, and the »an« is again held across the line break to the rhyme, just as »zog … an« was in the first stanza — the poem keeps doing this to him. »das Brünnchen« is the diminutive of »Brunnen«, the roadside well (the same »Brunnen« where the big dog was drinking).

sentences.t:
Er springt hinein. Die Not war groß;
es schießt der Has die Flinte los.
sentences.l:
He leaps in. The distress was great;
there shoots the hare the gun off.
sentences.i:
He leaps in. His plight was desperate;
and the hare fires off the gun.
sentences.n: »hinein« is the bare directional ‘in — into it’, doubling a direction that »springt« has already given: German likes the pair where English says only ‘leaps in.’ (Friedrich’s »Ins Bett muß … hinein« had it carrying the motion alone, with no motion verb at all.) »die Not« = ‘distress, dire straits’ — the word used of Friederich’s tormented cats. »losschießen« is separable: »schießt … los« = ‘lets fly, fires off’, with the placeholder »es« in front. Note what the poem does not say: it never tells you he got out.

sentences.t:
Des Jägers Frau am Fenster saß
und trank aus ihrer Kaffeetaß.
sentences.l:
The huntsman’s wife at-the window sat
and drank out of her coffee-cup.
sentences.i:
The huntsman’s wife sat at the window
drinking from her coffee cup.
sentences.n: »des Jägers Frau« puts the genitive in front of its noun, an old and faintly elevated order; today one would say »die Frau des Jägers«. »die Kaffeetaß« is »Kaffeetasse«, clipped. The scene jumps home without warning — a woman at her window with her afternoon coffee, and a shot already in the air.

sentences.t:
Die schoß das Häschen ganz entzwei;
da rief die Frau: »O wei! O wei!«
sentences.l:
That one, the little-hare shot quite in-two;
there cried the woman: “Oh woe! Oh woe!”
sentences.i:
The hare shot it clean in two,
and the woman cried: “Oh dear! Oh dear!”
sentences.n: »Die« at the head of the line is not ‘the’ but the demonstrative pronoun taking up the cup, fronted as the object; »das Häschen« is the subject. Neither word shows its case, so only the sense sorts them out — the cup cannot shoot the hare. »entzwei« = ‘in two, to pieces’. »O wei!« is the old cry of dismay behind »o weh«, and the poem gives her nothing else to say.

sentences.t:
Doch bei dem Brünnchen heimlich saß
des Häschens Kind, der kleine Has.
sentences.l:
But by the little-well secretly sat
the little-hare’s child, the little hare.
sentences.i:
But by the little well there sat, unnoticed,
the hare’s own child, the little hare.
sentences.n: The subject is held to the very end again, and the fronted »Doch bei dem Brünnchen« pulls you back to the well. »des Häschens Kind« repeats the pre-posed genitive of »des Jägers Frau« two lines before: the poem sets the two households side by side, each with someone at home. »heimlich« = ‘secretly, unnoticed’ — the word used of the parent hare stealing the gun.

sentences.t:
Der hockte da im grünen Gras;
dem floß der Kaffee auf die Nas.
sentences.l:
He crouched there in the green grass;
to-him flowed the coffee onto the nose.
sentences.i:
There he crouched in the green grass,
and the coffee ran down onto his nose.
sentences.n: »Der« and »dem« are the same demonstrative pronoun, first nominative then dative: ‘he …’, ‘and onto him …’. »dem floß der Kaffee auf die Nas« is the dative of the person plus the plain article, which is how German says ‘onto his nose.’ »hocken« = ‘to squat, crouch.’ And »im grünen Gras« is dative here — sitting, not moving into it, unlike the huntsman’s »ins grüne Gras«.

sentences.t:
Er schrie: »Wer hat mich da verbrannt?«
und hielt den Löffel in der Hand.
sentences.l:
He cried: “Who has me there burnt?”
and held the spoon in the hand.
sentences.i:
He cried: “Who has scalded me?”
and held the spoon in his hand.
sentences.n: »verbrennen« is ‘to burn’; of hot coffee, English says ‘scald’. »da« here is not ‘there’ but the vague ‘just now, on me’ of spoken German. The spoon is the joke and the whole ending: the young hare was having his own coffee, and objects only to the interruption. Nobody is punished and no lesson is drawn — the poem simply stops.
